summary:
On a long mission, help can be a light-minute away. Orbital Medic is the voice in the cabin until Mission Control answers.

A crewmate describes what they see in plain language: sudden chest pain, a chemical in the eye, someone who has collapsed. The monitor gathers the live signs already on the body — heart rate, oxygen, breathing, and blood pressure — and stays decision support: the next first-aid action and one question at a time, never a diagnosis. A ship map shows where the crewmate is. A camera can compare an eye still with a small labelled image set and file that guess as an experimental handoff. If the link fails, the same steps still run onboard.

The person who first notices a failing heart or a darkening eye is usually the astronaut beside them. This software gives that person something steady to hold in the minutes that matter most.
details:
Orbital Medic is a crew health monitor for the minutes when Earth cannot answer. A crewmate types what is happening in ordinary language — sudden chest pain, a chemical in the eye, a person who has collapsed — and the system replies with the next first-aid action and one question. Live heart rate, oxygen, breathing, and blood pressure stay on the screen beside a map of the ship, so the crew can see both the body and the place. The same guidance still runs if the link to Mission Control drops.

How it works. The home screen is a conversation, not a dashboard. Each reply keeps the urgency, the steps, the red flags, and a single missing fact: are they alert, which eye, what can they see. Quick replies let a gloved hand answer without typing. Naming a module on the ship flies the blueprint camera there. Choosing Spacecraft, Station, or Lunar Base changes the constraints: do not break a suit seal, watch lunar dust, start care before a comms reply. An optional Gemini model can phrase the guidance, but it cannot lower the urgency set by the onboard rules or introduce a drug dose. If the model is missing or fails, those rules answer instead. The eye camera stores a still for handoff and compares it with a small labelled set of eye images. That result is filed as an experimental similarity guess, not a measurement and not a diagnosis.

Benefits. Under stress, people do not hunt through menus. They say what they see. One question at a time keeps the crew moving while the steps stay visible. The monitor gathers the indicators already coming off the body and turns them into an action: call the medic, restrain, give oxygen only if trained, irrigate a chemical exposure, shield an injured eye. A checklist on screen lets the crew mark what is done. Contact Ground raises an alert with the crewmate and the module.

Intended impact. On a long mission the first person to notice a failing heart or a darkening eye is usually the astronaut beside them. Radio delay, isolation, and a closed vehicle mean that person may have to begin care alone. Orbital Medic is built for that gap. It does not replace Mission Control, a flight surgeon, or the vehicle checklist. It gives the crew a steady way to evaluate what they are seeing and act before the delay runs out. The demo path is a cardiovascular emergency and an eye injury, two problems a closed, altered-gravity environment makes both more likely and harder to hand off.

Tools. The app is TypeScript and React on Next.js, styled with Tailwind CSS. The ship blueprint is procedural Three.js, so no model file is required. Vitals charts use Recharts. Crew and alert state use Zustand. The offline medic rules are tested with Vitest. Gemini is optional. Supabase is optional for shared vitals; without it, a local simulator runs and the link shows as degraded. The eye screen was trained in Python with Pillow and NumPy on a labelled public image set, then exported so the website classifies a still in TypeScript. The only hardware is a laptop and a normal webcam.

What makes it different. Most health demos lead with a wall of numbers. This one leads with a voice. The creative constraint is safety: the software is not allowed to sound more certain than a trained crewmate with a checklist. The map, the camera, and the chat are one handoff, not three separate toys. The blueprint is drawn in code, in the same black and red as the rest of the cabin display, so the vehicle and the body read as one system.

What we considered. A frightened crewmate will speak in fragments, so the parser accepts plain speech and vitals written as “HR 110 RR 24 SpO2 94 pain 7.” A chest emergency must not be replaced by an eye photo. Guidance has to change between a station module and a lunar suit. Drug names and doses are refused. Every screen says this is decision support, not a diagnosis, not a prescription, and not an official NASA protocol. We would rather be the calm checklist in a quiet cabin than a confident answer that is wrong.
